title: Back-to-Back Procurement for IT Resellers: How to Turn Customer POs into Supplier POs Without Losing Margin
summary: How IT resellers turn customer POs into supplier POs from SKU-level price lists, enforce minimum-margin rules, and 3-way match supplier invoices.
body_markdown:
**TL;DR:** Back-to-back procurement means an IT reseller buys from its supplier only after a customer commits, so every supplier PO should be generated from a customer PO using the current price list and SKU-level discount. Margin leaks when price lists go stale, project discounts are applied on one side only, or supplier invoices arrive above the PO price. A minimum-margin rule at PO stage plus 3-way matching at invoice stage closes those gaps, even for small resellers handling 20 to 50 supplier invoices a month.


Most IT resellers do not lose money on a big, visible mistake. They lose it on a laptop order quoted from last quarter’s price list, an accessory discount assumed but never applied, or a supplier invoice a few dollars per unit above the PO. None of these trip an alarm; they surface weeks later as a gross margin that does not match what sales reported.


This guide is for IT solution providers and resellers that buy from regular suppliers on fixed price lists and resell hardware, licences and services to business customers. It covers turning customer POs into supplier POs, keeping price lists usable, and enforcing a margin floor automatically, even for a lean team handling a few dozen invoices a month.


## What Is Back-to-Back Procurement?


Back-to-back procurement is a purchasing model in which a reseller raises a supplier purchase order only after receiving a confirmed customer order, and each supplier PO maps directly to that customer order. The reseller holds little or no speculative stock, and the profit on each deal equals the customer price minus the supplier cost on that matched pair.


For IT resellers, this is the default. A customer orders notebooks, docking stations and a support pack; the reseller confirms, then buys hardware from a distributor and the support pack from the vendor. Larger ERPs formalise this pattern. Microsoft documents it as[drop shipment in Business Central](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dynamics365/business-central/sales-how-drop-shipment) , where a purchase order is linked to the originating sales order.


The model is low-risk on inventory but high-risk on pricing: any gap between assumed and actual cost comes straight out of margin.


## Where Does Margin Leak Between the Customer PO and the Supplier PO?


Margin leaks at four points: when the quote uses an outdated cost, when a project discount is applied to the sell price but not secured on the buy price, when the supplier PO is keyed with a different price or quantity, and when the supplier invoice exceeds the PO. Each is a manual handoff with no automatic check.


Here is how those leak points typically show up in a reseller with a small sales and operations team.


Leak point What goes wrong Typical root cause Control that catches it


Quote stage Price quoted below true cost Salesperson uses an old price list or forgets the SKU discount tier Quote checked against current item master cost


Project pricing Customer gets a project price, reseller pays standard cost Vendor deal registration not approved, expired, or not referenced on the PO Project prices stored with validity date and deal reference


PO creation Supplier PO keyed with wrong SKU, quantity or price Retyping from the customer PO into the accounting system PO generated from customer order lines, not retyped


Invoice stage Supplier bills above PO price Price increase, freight added, or substitution not flagged 3-way match with price tolerance before payment


Month end Margin report does not match reality Buy and sell lines are not linked, so margin is estimated Every supplier PO carries the customer order reference


The common thread is that the sell side and the buy side live in different places, so nobody sees both sides of the deal at once.


## Why Do Supplier Price Lists and SKU-Level Discounts Cause So Many Errors?


Supplier price lists cause errors because the reseller’s real cost is not printed on them. It is list price minus a discount that differs by SKU or product family, sometimes overridden by a project price. That cost has to be calculated, and it changes whenever the supplier reissues the list or the deal terms change.


For example, a distributor publishes a monthly PDF list, and the reseller gets 25 percent off notebooks and 30 percent off accessories. A specific bid may also carry a vendor-approved project price valid for 90 days.


Three practical problems follow:


- **Format chaos.** Each supplier uses its own layout, often PDF, so re-keying happens irregularly and the spreadsheet drifts out of date.
- **Discount tables live in people’s heads.** A new salesperson may quote at the wrong tier, or assume a discount that does not exist.
- **Project prices outlive their validity.** A special price for one bid gets reused for a different customer.


The fix is an item master that holds, per supplier and SKU, the list price, the applicable discount, the resulting net cost, and any project prices tagged with an expiry date and deal reference. Peakflo’s[procure-to-pay platform](https://peakflo.co/accounts-payable) lets teams bulk upload price lists in any format, including PDF, using AI document capture, so refreshing the list each month becomes a review task rather than a typing task.


Once the item master exists, the difference between the three cost types becomes explicit, as the table below shows.


Cost type How it is calculated When it applies Main risk if mishandled


Standard net cost List price minus standard SKU or family discount Default for any order Stale list price after supplier update


Project price Fixed price agreed with vendor for a named deal Only for the registered customer and validity window Reused after expiry or for the wrong customer


Spot price One-off price quoted by supplier for a specific order Out-of-list items or short supply Not recorded, so invoice cannot be checked


## How Do You Turn a Customer PO into a Supplier PO Automatically?


To convert a customer PO into a supplier PO automatically, match each customer order line to a SKU in your item master, apply vendor selection rules to choose the supplier, look up that supplier’s current net cost, and generate a draft supplier PO that references the customer order. Margin validation and approval then run before the PO is released.


The process breaks into four steps.


### 1. Capture the customer order


Customer POs arrive as PDFs or emails. AI capture reads the customer name, PO number, line items, quantities and agreed prices. If your customer uses its own part numbers, those need mapping to your SKUs. That mapping problem is covered in depth in our guide to[customer PO to sales order automation and product code mismatch](https://peakflo.co/blog/customer-po-to-sales-order-automation-product-code-mismatch) , so it is not repeated here.


### 2. Select the vendor by rule


Common vendor selection rules include:


- Preferred supplier by product family, for example all notebooks from distributor A
- Project-registered supplier where a deal registration exists for this customer
- Lowest current net cost among approved suppliers for commodity items
- Fallback supplier when the preferred one has flagged a stock shortage


These rules can be expressed in a no-code rules engine rather than left to individual judgement.


### 3. Generate the draft supplier PO


For each selected supplier, the system builds a PO with the matched SKUs, quantities and net cost, plus the customer PO number as a reference. One customer order may produce several supplier POs. Accounting systems such as Xero support[purchase orders natively](https://www.xero.com/sg/accounting-software/purchase-orders/) , and the draft can be pushed into them through the standard[Xero purchase orders API](https://developer.xero.com/documentation/api/accounting/purchaseorders) once approved.


### 4. Validate and approve


Before release, the PO passes a margin check and, if needed, an approval route. Small resellers often skip this step, yet it is the one that protects profit.


If your challenge is pulling purchase prices from a CRM in a manufacturing context rather than from supplier price lists, our article on[automated SO to PO with CRM price validation](https://peakflo.co/blog/automated-so-to-po-crm-price-validation-manufacturing) covers that variation.


## How Should Minimum-Margin Validation Rules Work?


A minimum-margin validation rule compares the selling price on the customer order with the expected supplier cost for each line and for the order as a whole, and blocks or escalates the supplier PO when margin falls below a defined floor. The floor is a policy decision, often around 15 to 25 percent for hardware, set by product family or customer tier.


A good rule set distinguishes lines that are deliberately thin, such as a notebook bundled with a profitable support contract, from lines that are thin by accident. Checking at both line and order level handles this, as in this illustrative rule set.


```text
Rule: Back-to-back margin floor
FOR each supplier PO line:
expected_cost = project_price IF valid for this customer and date
ELSE list_price x (1 - SKU discount)
line_margin   = (customer_price - expected_cost) / customer_price
IF order_margin < 20%            -> BLOCK, route to Director
IF any line_margin < 0%          -> BLOCK, route to Sales Manager
IF any line_margin between 0-10%  -> FLAG, require reason code
IF project_price used AND expired -> BLOCK, recalculate at standard cost
ELSE                              -> RELEASE PO to supplier
```


A few design principles make these rules work in practice:


- **Use expected cost, not last paid cost.** Read current terms from the item master, not history.
- **Require a reason for exceptions.** Strategic thin deals should be documented, not quietly approved.
- **Route to the person who owns the price.** Project exceptions go to whoever negotiated the project price.
- **Keep it visible.** Show calculated margin on the approval screen.


This kind of preventive control aligns with the internal control principles in the[COSO Internal Control framework](https://www.coso.org/guidance-on-ic) , which emphasises control activities embedded in the process rather than detective reviews after the fact.


## Why Does 3-Way Matching Matter So Much for Resellers?


Three-way matching compares the supplier PO, the goods receipt and the supplier invoice before payment. For a reseller, it is the final margin check, because it confirms the supplier billed at the cost used to validate margin and delivered what the customer ordered. Without it, an invoice price increase erodes margin after approval.


Distributors adjust prices between order and invoice, add freight lines, substitute models, or ship partially and bill in full. A sensible setup uses a tight price tolerance, quantity matching against receipts, flags for invoice lines not on the PO, and routing of mismatches to the person who raised the PO.


Our detailed guide to[three-way matching in accounts payable](https://peakflo.co/blog/three-way-matching-accounts-payable) explains tolerance design, and the companion piece on[AI agents for three-way matching](https://peakflo.co/blog/ai-agents-three-way-matching-purchase-order-reconciliation-guide) covers how exceptions are resolved automatically.


The table below shows what each match outcome means for a back-to-back deal and the appropriate action.


Match outcome What it usually means Recommended action


PO, receipt and invoice agree Deal closed at validated margin Approve for payment automatically


Invoice price above PO Supplier price change or wrong discount applied Hold, query supplier, recalculate margin


Invoice quantity above receipt Billed for undelivered goods Hold until remaining goods are received


Extra invoice line not on PO Freight, handling or substitution Route to buyer to accept or dispute


Invoice below PO Supplier applied a better price Approve and update item master if ongoing


## Do Small Resellers Processing 20 to 50 Invoices a Month Really Need This?


Yes. Small resellers need procurement controls because exposure depends on deal value, not invoice count. A team handling 20 to 50 supplier invoices a month may still move significant sums on each one, and typically has no segregation of duties to catch pricing errors. Automated rules provide the second pair of eyes that a small team lacks.


Automation is often assumed to pay off only above a few hundred invoices a month. That holds for data entry savings, not for margin protection. For example, a four-person reseller processing around 30 supplier invoices a month worth several thousand dollars each only needs one order a month quoted at the wrong discount tier for the annual leak to exceed the cost of a procurement tool.


Small teams also face specific control weaknesses:


- **One person does everything.** The same person quotes, raises the PO and approves the invoice. Fraud examiners consistently identify a lack of segregation of duties as a leading weakness in small organisations, as noted in the[ACFE Report to the Nations](https://www.acfe.com/fraud-resources/report-to-the-nations) .
- **Knowledge is concentrated.** When the person who knows the discount tiers is away, errors rise.
- **Cash is tight.** Overpaying an invoice ties up working capital needed for the next order.

See our[grant overview](https://peakflo.co/productivity-solutions-grant) for eligibility details.


## How Does Back-to-Back Procurement Affect Compliance and Cash?


Back-to-back procurement affects compliance because every supplier purchase and customer sale must be documented, linked and taxed correctly, and it affects cash because supplier payment terms rarely line up with customer payment terms. Linked documents make GST reporting, audits and cash planning far simpler.


On the compliance side, a supplier PO that references its customer order creates an audit trail showing why a purchase was made. For GST-registered businesses in Singapore, accurate input tax claims depend on valid supplier invoices that match what was purchased, as set out in[IRAS guidance on GST](https://www.iras.gov.sg/taxes/goods-services-tax-%28gst%29) . Resellers selling to government agencies or large enterprises may also need to issue e-invoices through the[InvoiceNow network](https://www.imda.gov.sg/how-we-can-help/nationwide-e-invoicing-framework) , which is easier when sell-side data is structured rather than typed.


On the cash side, a reseller may pay the distributor in 30 days while the customer pays in 60. Linked buy and sell lines show committed margin and cash per deal instead of month-end estimates.

## Our Verdict: When Is Back-to-Back Procurement Automation Worth It?


### Automate back-to-back procurement if


- You buy from regular suppliers on price lists with SKU or family-level discounts
- Supplier price lists arrive as PDFs and are re-keyed by hand, or not at all
- You have quoted or delivered at least one deal below cost in the past year
- Vendor project prices or deal registrations are tracked in email or memory
- The same person quotes, raises POs and approves supplier invoices
- Month-end gross margin regularly differs from what sales expected


### Manual handling may still be workable if


- You sell mostly services with little third-party hardware
- Each deal is large and bespoke, and you have a dedicated buyer reviewing every one
- You buy from a single supplier at fixed net prices with no discount tiers


**Our Recommendation:** If you resell third-party hardware or licences on discount-based price lists, put a minimum-margin rule at PO stage and 3-way matching at invoice stage before anything else. These two controls catch the majority of margin leakage, and they matter as much at 30 invoices a month as at 300. ## Conclusion


Back-to-back procurement keeps inventory risk low but moves the risk to pricing, and pricing errors are quiet. A stale price list, an assumed discount, an expired project price or an unchecked invoice each erode margin unnoticed until the books close.


The answer is a connected flow: price lists in an item master, vendor rules, supplier POs generated from customer orders, margin validated before release, and invoices matched before payment. Together, they turn a margin policy into a control that runs on every deal. ## Frequently Asked Questions


### What is back-to-back procurement?


Back-to-back procurement is a buying model where a reseller only purchases from a supplier after a customer has committed to an order. Each supplier purchase order is raised against a specific customer purchase order, so stock is not held speculatively and the margin on each deal is the difference between the customer price and the supplier cost on that matched pair.


### Why do IT resellers lose margin in back-to-back deals?


Margin usually leaks in three places: the salesperson quotes from an outdated or wrong supplier price list, a project-specific discount is applied on the sell side but not reflected on the buy side, or the supplier invoices at a higher price than the PO and nobody checks. Each error is small, but on thin hardware margins a few of them can wipe out a month of profit.


### What is a minimum-margin validation rule?


A minimum-margin validation rule is an automated check that compares the customer selling price with the expected supplier cost for each line or order and blocks or escalates the transaction if margin falls below a set floor, for example 20 percent. It turns a pricing policy that lives in people’s heads into a control that runs on every order.


### How do supplier price list discounts work for IT resellers?


Distributors and vendors typically publish a list price per SKU and grant the reseller a discount off list that varies by product family, for example 25 percent on notebooks and 30 percent on accessories. Some deals also carry a project or bid-specific price that overrides the standard discount. The reseller’s true cost is list price minus the applicable discount, so the discount table must be maintained alongside the list.


### Can a supplier price list in PDF format be imported automatically?


Yes. Modern AI document capture can read price lists in PDF, Excel or CSV format, extract SKU, description, list price and discount columns, and load them into an item master for review. A person should still check the extracted list before it goes live, especially when the supplier changes the layout of its file.


### How is a customer PO converted into a supplier PO?


The customer PO lines are matched to items in the reseller’s item master. For each item, vendor selection rules decide which supplier to buy from, the system looks up the cost from that supplier’s current price list and discount, and a draft supplier PO is generated with a reference back to the customer order. The draft then passes margin validation and approval before it is sent.


### What does 3-way matching add to back-to-back procurement?


Three-way matching compares the supplier PO, the goods receipt and the supplier invoice before payment. In a back-to-back model it confirms that the supplier delivered what the customer ordered and billed at the price used to calculate margin. Without it, an invoice price increase silently eats the margin that was validated at PO stage.


### Do small resellers with 20 to 50 invoices a month need procurement controls?


Yes. Low volume does not mean low value. A reseller processing a few dozen supplier invoices a month may have average deal values in the thousands, and a single underpriced project can cost more than a year of software fees. Small teams also lack segregation of duties, so automated rules provide a check that headcount cannot.


### Should margin be validated at quote stage or at PO stage?


Ideally both. A quote-stage check stops a salesperson promising a price below cost, while a PO-stage check catches changes made between quote and order, such as a revised supplier price or an added discount. The PO-stage check is the more important of the two because it uses the actual supplier and cost that will be committed.


### What happens when a project discount from a vendor expires?


If the project price expires and the item master still holds it, the reseller will calculate margin against a cost it can no longer get, and the supplier invoice will arrive higher than expected. Storing project prices with a validity date and a deal reference, and falling back to the standard discount when they lapse, prevents this.


### Which accounting systems support back-to-back purchase orders?


Most mid-market ERPs, including Microsoft Dynamics 365 Business Central and NetSuite, offer drop shipment or special order features that link a purchase order to a sales order. Small business accounting tools such as Xero support purchase orders but have lighter linking and no native margin floor, which is why many resellers add a procurement layer on top.
